Ghana er en republikk i Vest-Afrika som ligger ved Guineabukta.
Ghana is a republic in West Africa situated on the Gulf of Guinea.

1000053.etyen:
Borrowed from English Ghana, the name adopted by the former Gullkysten (“Gold Coast”) when it became independent from the United Kingdom in 1957.
The modern country was named after Ghanariket (“Ghana Empire”), a medieval West African state situated considerably farther northwest than present-day Ghana, principally in areas of what are now Mauritania, Mali and Senegal. The Soninke name of the medieval polity is commonly given as Wagadu. Medieval Arabic sources record غانا (Ḡānā) as the name of a ruler and, by extension, of the city or country he ruled.

en.g: An adjective-forming suffix occurring chiefly in learned and borrowed words, expressing that something belongs to, is characteristic of or resembles what is indicated by the base

1000309.etyen:
Borrowed from French -in (“of or pertaining to”), from Latin -īnus (“of or pertaining to”), from Proto-Italic *-īnos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *-iHnos. Some learned formations also reflect Ancient Greek -ινος (-inos, “of or pertaining to”).
Compare Danish -in and Swedish -in, as well as English -ine, French -in and German -in (“adjective-forming suffix”).

a male given name from German, equivalent to English John

1001077.etyen:
Borrowed from German Johann (“male given name”), a short form of Johannes (“male given name”), ultimately from Latin Iōhannēs (“male given name”), from Ancient Greek Ἰωάννης (Iōánnēs, “male given name”), from Hebrew יוֹחָנָן (Yōḥānān, “Yahweh is gracious”).
Compare Danish Johann, Swedish Johann, Finnish Johann, Icelandic Jóhann and Faroese Jóhann (“male given names”).

en.g: a thin soup, especially one made with meat or meat broth
x: spa er en gammel, tradisjonsrik rett fra Telemark
Spa is an old dish with a long tradition in Telemark.

1001589.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse spað (“thin soup made from meat or fish”). According to a traditional etymology, the Old Norse noun ultimately belongs to the Proto-Indo-European root *speh₁- (“to stretch, spread out”), with the proposed semantic development “stretched out” → “thin”.
First attested in 1852 in Dano-Norwegian, under the pronunciation-based spelling spa, in Nicolai Ramm Østgaard’s En Fjeldbygd.
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk spa (“thin soup”), Old Swedish spadh, Swedish spad (“broth, cooking liquid”), Danish spad (“broth, thin meat soup”) and Icelandic spað (“finely chopped meat”).

Last part from French officier (“officer”), from Old French officer, officier (“officer”), from Medieval Latin officiārius (“officer”), from officium (“duty, service, office”), a contraction of opificium (“work”), an old derivative of ops, opis (“power, ability, resources”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ep-(i)-, *h₃op-(i)- (“force, ability”), from *h₃ep- (“to work, toil, make; ability, force”).

1004661.etyen:
From pinne (“stick”) + brød (“bread”). The name refers to the stick around which a strip of dough is wound before being baked over a fire. First attested in 1989.
Compare Swedish pinnbröd (“stick bread, campfire bread”).

en.g: grand duchy; a state, territory or domain ruled by a grand duke or grand duchess
x: Luxembourg er verdens eneste gjenværende storhertugdømme.
Luxembourg is the world's only remaining grand duchy.
Heidelberg … ligger i Neckardalen i storhertugdømmet Baden
Heidelberg … lies in the Neckar valley in the Grand Duchy of Baden.

1004917.etyen:
From storhertug (“grand duke”) + -dømme (“domain, area of rule”), literally “domain of a grand duke”. The suffix -dømme (“domain, area of rule or authority”) is from Old Norse dǿmi, ultimately related to Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- (“to put, place”).
Compare the parallel formations Norwegian Nynorsk storhertugdøme, Danish storhertugdømme, Swedish storhertigdöme, Icelandic stórhertogadæmi, Faroese stórhertugadømi, Dutch groothertogdom and German Großherzogtum (“grand duchy”).
